subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How does Tybalt's character drive the play's theme of love versus hate?
options: His fierce hatred of the Montagues fuels the violence that dooms the lovers
questions.explain: Tybalt's aggressive hatred of Montagues sparks the duel that kills Mercutio and gets Romeo banished.

questions.q: Why does Romeo kill himself in the Capulet tomb?
options: He is mortally wounded by Paris
He believes Juliet is truly dead
He is ordered to by the Prince
questions.explain: Believing Juliet dead because he never received the Friar's message, Romeo drinks poison beside her.

questions.q: How does Juliet die at the end of the play?
options: She stabs herself with Romeo's dagger
She drinks the Friar's potion again
questions.explain: Waking to find Romeo dead, Juliet stabs herself with his dagger.

questions.q: Which contemporary event involving a plot against King James influences the play's themes of treason and regicide?
questions.explain: The 1605 Gunpowder Plot to kill James I made treason and regicide especially resonant for Jacobean audiences.

questions.q: What good comes from the lovers' deaths at the play's close?
options: The Prince seizes both family estates
Verona is freed from the plague
questions.explain: The grieving families finally end their feud, reconciled by the tragedy they caused.

questions.q: What plan does Friar Lawrence give Juliet to avoid marrying Paris?
options: To run away to Mantua alone
To drink a potion that makes her appear dead
To confess the secret marriage publicly
questions.explain: He gives her a sleeping potion to feign death so she can later escape with Romeo.

questions.q: After Duncan names his successor, who does Macbeth see as an obstacle to the throne?
questions.explain: Duncan declares Malcolm the Prince of Cumberland and heir, a step Macbeth must "o'erleap" to become king.

questions.q: What does Macbeth hallucinate seeing before he murders Duncan?
options: A dagger leading him toward the chamber
questions.explain: He asks "Is this a dagger which I see before me?", a vision drawing him to commit the murder.

questions.q: Why does Macbeth have Banquo murdered after becoming king?
options: The witches prophesied Banquo's descendants would be kings
questions.explain: The witches foretold Banquo would father a line of kings, so Macbeth fears him and orders his death.

questions.q: In the famous balcony scene, what does Juliet mean by "wherefore art thou Romeo?"
options: She questions whether he is real
She wonders why he loves her
She asks where Romeo is hiding
She laments that he is a Montague, an enemy of her family
questions.explain: "Wherefore" means "why"; Juliet wishes Romeo were not a Montague so their families' feud would not divide them.

questions.q: What prophecy gives Macbeth false confidence that no man can harm him?
options: That Banquo's heirs will spare him
That he will reign for forty years
That none of woman born shall harm him
That the witches will protect him
questions.explain: He believes "none of woman born" can kill him, until Macduff reveals he was born by Caesarean.

questions.q: Which character secretly marries Romeo and Juliet, hoping to end the feud?
questions.explain: Friar Lawrence weds them in secret, believing their union may reconcile the two families.

questions.q: In Romeo and Juliet, at whose party do Romeo and Juliet first meet?
questions.explain: Romeo gatecrashes the Capulets' masked ball, where he meets Juliet and instantly falls in love.

questions.q: In Macbeth, what do the three witches prophesy will happen to Macbeth at the start of the play?
options: He will become Thane of Cawdor and then king
He will die in battle against Norway
He will father a line of kings
He will be banished from Scotland
questions.explain: The witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and one who shall be king hereafter.

questions.q: Whose murder does Macbeth carry out to seize the throne?
questions.explain: Macbeth murders King Duncan in his sleep at Inverness to take the crown.

questions.q: How does the Elizabethan belief in fate and the stars shape the play's tone?
options: It implies the feud can never end
It frames the lovers as "star-crossed", doomed by forces beyond their control
It suggests the lovers freely control their destiny
It shows religion has no role
questions.explain: Elizabethan audiences believed the stars influenced human lives, so the "star-crossed" lovers seem fated for tragedy.

questions.q: In Romeo and Juliet, which two feuding families does the play centre on?
questions.explain: The ancient grudge between the Montagues and Capulets frames the tragedy.

questions.q: How does Mercutio mock the idea of fate and dreams before his death?
options: With his cynical Queen Mab speech
questions.explain: Mercutio's witty Queen Mab speech ridicules dreams as meaningless, contrasting with the play's sense of fate.

questions.q: In Romeo and Juliet, which character urges calm and tries to keep the peace, refusing to fight Tybalt before Mercutio intervenes?
questions.explain: Romeo refuses to fight the newly-related Tybalt, prompting Mercutio to duel in his place.

questions.q: Whom does Lord Capulet intend Juliet to marry, against her wishes?
questions.explain: Capulet arranges for Juliet to marry the wealthy young Count Paris, brushing aside her secret marriage to Romeo.

questions.q: Which character ultimately kills Macbeth in the final battle?
questions.explain: Macduff, who was "from his mother's womb untimely ripp'd", slays Macbeth and so fulfils the prophecy.

questions.q: Whose ghost appears to Macbeth at the banquet, terrifying him in front of his guests?
questions.explain: Banquo, murdered on Macbeth's orders, returns as a ghost only Macbeth can see at the feast.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE English Literature (1ET0) specification; Paper 1 Shakespeare And Post 1914 Literature
